Across 37 studies, lifelong non-smoking women with a smoking husband had a pooled odds ratio of 1.24 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.36) for lung cancer.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pooled odds ratio (OR), random-effects model, DL tau2 | 1.24 | 1.13 to 1.36 | k = 37 studies; one n = one study row (cohort or case-control comparison) | z test, p = 5.65e-06 | fit_meta_analysis |
| Cochran Q (heterogeneity) | 47.50 on 36 df | not applicable | 37 studies | chi-square, p = 0.095 | fit_meta_analysis |
| I2 (share of variation from heterogeneity) | 24.2% | not applicable | 37 studies | not applicable | fit_meta_analysis |
| tau2 (between-study variance) | 0.0170 (SE 0.0171) | not applicable | 37 studies | not applicable | fit_meta_analysis |
| Prediction interval for a new study (OR) | 0.94 to 1.63 | not applicable | 37 studies | not applicable | fit_meta_analysis |
| Egger test for small-study effects | t = 2.38 on 35 df | not applicable | 37 studies | Egger regression, p = 0.023 | funnel_and_egger |
| Participants | not in file | not applicable | not applicable | not applicable | not applicable |

Uncertain:
- Egger test p = 0.023 suggests asymmetry. The cause can be publication bias, true heterogeneity or chance.
- Five study labels appear twice (Garfinkel, Lam, Kabat, Brownson, Liu). I treated each row as one independent replicate. If rows share participants, the interval is too narrow.
- Effects are odds ratios. Lung cancer is rare, so the OR is close to the risk ratio, but it is not one.

Waits for you: Nothing.
